topics.title: What Rhetoric Is
topics.short: Rhetoric is the art of using language to inform, persuade or move an audience. Aristotle defined it as the ability to see, in any case, the available means of persuasion.
topics.trouble: Learners hear rhetoric only as an insult (“empty rhetoric”) and miss that it is the study of how all writing and speech work on an audience.

topics.title: The Rhetorical Situation
topics.short: The writer, the audience, the purpose, the context (the occasion and the need that calls for the text) and the message shape every choice a writer makes.
topics.trouble: Learners analyze a text without asking who it was for and when it was written, and so misjudge its choices.

topics.title: Ethos: The Speaker’s Character
topics.short: Ethos persuades through the character the speaker shows: good sense, good character and goodwill toward the audience.
topics.trouble: Learners think ethos means quoting an expert. For Aristotle it is the trust the speech itself earns; a writer builds it with fairness, knowledge and respect for the reader.

topics.title: Pathos: The Audience’s Emotions
topics.short: Pathos persuades by putting the audience in a frame of mind, through stories, images and word choice.
topics.trouble: Learners treat every appeal to emotion as a trick. Emotion that fits the facts is a fair part of persuasion; it becomes a fallacy when it replaces the reasons.

topics.title: Logos: The Reasoning
topics.short: Logos persuades through the argument itself: evidence, examples and reasoning that show a claim is true or likely.
topics.trouble: Learners call any number logos, even a frightening statistic used without context.

topics.title: Identifying Appeals
topics.short: Most passages blend the appeals. Decide which one each sentence leans on most, and how they work together.
topics.trouble: Learners look for one label for a whole passage instead of seeing how ethos, pathos and logos support each other.

topics.title: Kairos: The Right Moment
topics.short: Kairos is the fitting moment: an argument works when it suits its time, place and audience.
topics.trouble: Learners ignore timing. The same words can persuade one week and fall flat the next.

topics.title: Kinds of Claims
topics.short: Claims of fact (is it so?), of value (is it good or bad?) and of policy (what should we do?).
topics.trouble: Learners confuse a claim of value with a claim of fact because both use is (“Homework is useless” is a judgment, not a measurement).

topics.title: Patterns of Reasoning
topics.short: Arguments reason from examples (induction), from general principles (deduction), from cause and effect, from comparison and from analogy.
topics.trouble: Learners can’t say how an argument gets from its evidence to its claim, so they can’t judge whether the step is strong.

topics.title: The Toulmin Model
topics.short: Stephen Toulmin’s model: a claim, the grounds (data) offered for it, and the warrant that links them, with backing, a qualifier and a rebuttal.
topics.trouble: Learners mix up grounds and warrant. The grounds are the specific evidence; the warrant is the general principle, often unstated, that lets the evidence support the claim.

topics.title: Finding Unstated Warrants
topics.short: State the general principle an argument takes for granted, then ask whether the audience would accept it.
topics.trouble: Learners restate the claim and call it the warrant.

topics.title: Qualifiers and Limits
topics.short: Words like usually, most and probably make a claim match its evidence.
topics.trouble: Learners think qualifying a claim weakens it. An overstated claim is easier to knock down.

topics.title: Weighing Evidence
topics.short: Good evidence is relevant, sufficient, accurate, current where that matters, and fairly represented.
topics.trouble: Learners count pieces of evidence instead of weighing how well each one supports the claim.

topics.title: Counterarguments
topics.short: State the strongest opposing view fairly, in terms its supporters would accept, before you answer it.
topics.trouble: Learners answer the weakest objection (a straw man), or leave out the other side entirely.

topics.title: Concession and Rebuttal
topics.short: Concede what is true in the other view, then rebut what you can: “Granted, …; but …”
topics.trouble: Learners concede so much that their own claim disappears, or rebut by attacking the people on the other side.

topics.title: The Classical Arrangement
topics.short: The classical oration: introduction (exordium), background (narratio), the claim and its parts (partitio), proof (confirmatio), answers to objections (refutatio) and conclusion (peroratio).
topics.trouble: Learners think there is one fixed order for an argument. The classical parts are a toolkit: writers move the refutation earlier or later to suit the audience.

topics.title: Fallacies in Arguments
topics.short: Spot common fallacies in real writing, by the Logic Ladder’s names: attacking the person, straw man, false dilemma, hasty generalization, slippery slope and others.
topics.trouble: Learners call any argument they disagree with a fallacy. A fallacy is a flaw in the reasoning, not a conclusion you dislike.

topics.title: A Defensible Thesis
topics.short: An argument’s thesis takes a position that reasonable people could dispute, and that you can defend with evidence.
topics.trouble: Learners write a thesis no one would dispute (a fact) or one no evidence could support (a pure preference).

topics.title: The Argument Essay
topics.short: A defensible thesis, a line of reasoning, evidence with commentary, and an answer to the other side, in an order that builds.
topics.trouble: Learners summarize evidence without commentary that ties it to the claim.

topics.title: Line of Reasoning and Commentary
topics.short: Commentary explains how each piece of evidence supports the claim, and the reasons build on each other in a logical order.
topics.trouble: Learners let quotations speak for themselves, so the reader must guess how they support the point.

topics.title: Rhetorical Analysis
topics.short: Rhetorical analysis explains how a writer’s choices serve a purpose for an audience. It doesn’t argue whether you agree.
topics.trouble: Learners summarize the text, or argue with it, instead of explaining how it works on its audience.

topics.title: Choices and Effects
topics.short: Name a choice (a story, a contrast, a repetition), then explain its effect on the audience and how it serves the purpose.
topics.trouble: Learners list devices (feature spotting) without saying why they matter.

topics.title: Common Rhetorical Devices
topics.short: Anaphora, antithesis, parallelism, rhetorical questions, analogy, understatement and other patterns writers use on purpose.
topics.trouble: Learners think naming a device is the analysis. The name is the start; the effect is the point.

topics.title: Tone and Shifts in Tone
topics.short: Tone is the writer’s attitude, shown by diction and sentence structure. Analysis often turns on where the tone shifts.
topics.trouble: Learners name a tone with a vague word (positive, negative) instead of a precise one (wry, urgent, reverent).

topics.title: A Thesis for Rhetorical Analysis
topics.short: Name the writer, the purpose and the main strategies, and say how they serve the purpose.
topics.trouble: Learners write a thesis that only lists devices (“She uses ethos, pathos and logos”).

topics.title: The Rhetorical Analysis Essay
topics.short: Organize by the writer’s strategies or by the text’s sections, with short quotations and commentary on each.
topics.trouble: Learners organize by appeal (one paragraph each for ethos, pathos and logos) instead of following the writer’s moves.

topics.title: Reading Sources Together
topics.short: Find where sources agree, where they disagree, and where they answer different questions.
topics.trouble: Learners summarize sources one at a time instead of putting them in conversation.

topics.title: Working Sources into Your Sentences
topics.short: Use signal phrases, partial quotations, brackets for changes and ellipses for cuts, so sources fit your sentences smoothly.
topics.trouble: Learners change a quotation’s words without brackets, or cut words without an ellipsis.

topics.title: The Synthesis Essay
topics.short: Use several sources to support your own argument, with citations. The sources serve your claim; they don’t make it for you.
topics.trouble: Learners let the sources organize the essay (one paragraph per source) instead of organizing by their own reasons.

topics.title: Diction
topics.short: Choose words for precision, connotation and the right level of formality.
topics.trouble: Learners pick a thesaurus word whose connotation doesn’t fit (thrifty and stingy both mean careful with money, but only one is praise).

topics.title: Concision
topics.short: Omit needless words: cut redundancy, empty phrases, and weak openings like “There is” and “It is.”
topics.trouble: Learners think longer sounds smarter, so they pad sentences with phrases that add no meaning.

topics.title: Active and Passive Voice, Used Well
topics.short: Prefer the active voice when the doer matters. Use the passive when the doer is unknown or unimportant, or to keep the focus on what was acted on.
topics.trouble: Learners are told never to use the passive, and force awkward active sentences; or they use the passive to hide who did something.

topics.title: Sentence Variety
topics.short: Vary sentence length and structure: short sentences for emphasis, longer ones for connected ideas.
topics.trouble: Learners start every sentence with the subject, or write every sentence the same length.

topics.title: Emphasis and Word Order
topics.short: Put the words you most want remembered at the end of a sentence, where readers give them the most weight.
topics.trouble: Learners bury the key word in the middle, or end on a weak phrase like “in today’s society.”

topics.title: Old Information Before New
topics.short: Begin a sentence with what the reader already knows and end with what is new, so each sentence hands off to the next.
topics.trouble: Learners jump to a new topic at the start of every sentence, so the prose feels choppy even when each sentence is correct.

topics.title: Formal and Informal Register
topics.short: Match the register to the audience: contractions, slang, and person (I, you, one) all signal formality.
topics.trouble: Learners think formal writing means long words and the passive voice. Clear, plain words are formal enough for almost any reader.

topics.title: Figures of Speech
topics.short: Metaphor, simile, personification, hyperbole and understatement, chosen for their effect.
topics.trouble: Learners mix metaphors, or reach for clichés that no longer make a picture.

topics.title: Classic Style Advice
topics.short: Strunk’s Elements of Style (1918) gave rules like “Omit needless words” and “Use the active voice.” Know what the advice is for and when good writers break it.
topics.trouble: Learners treat rules of thumb as laws. Strunk himself wrote that the best writers sometimes break the rules, for some compensating merit.

topics.title: Reading a Prompt
topics.short: Find the task word (analyze, argue, explain), the subject, and any limits before you plan.
topics.trouble: Learners answer the topic instead of the task: they argue when the prompt asks them to analyze.

topics.title: Timed Writing
topics.short: Read the prompt closely, plan for a few minutes, write a clear thesis, and save time to reread.
topics.trouble: Learners start writing at once and drift away from the prompt, or run out of time before the conclusion.

topics.title: The College Application Essay
topics.short: A personal essay shows who you are through a specific story and what you made of it, in your own voice.
topics.trouble: Learners list achievements (a résumé in paragraphs) instead of telling one story and reflecting on what it shows.
